summary:
# Summary of Brother Luca's Fragmentary Notebooks

This text comprises twenty pages from the notebooks of Brother Luca, a Renaissance Franciscan friar who serves as sacristan, librarian, and workshop overseer at a convent in Sansepolcro. The fragments, dated across the present year, reveal a man torn between mathematical rapture and monastic discipline, between aesthetic joy and spiritual duty.

The collection opens with a confession delivered before chapter on Friday: Luca accuses himself of finding greater gladness in geometric contemplation than in prayer. During Sext-hour, he counts the twelve petals of the rose-window six times over, delighting in the constancy of the number. At the elevation of the Host, his mind sees nested circles and inscribed squares rather than devotion. In his breviary at Psalm 103, he has pricked five margin notches representing Plato's five regular solids. Father Bartolomeo assigns him penance with the pointed instruction not to count his prayer beads—an admonition Luca confesses he has failed to obey, though he has at least stopped counting aloud.

The ledger entries reveal Luca's meticulous financial stewardship. He records payments to the muleteer Bartolo for transporting printer's equipment from Sansepolcro to Bologna, tracks the compound interest on Donna Beatrice's legacy at the Monte dei Paschi bank in Siena (calculated at six percent), and maintains balanced books that reconcile perfectly at two hundred twelve florins, six scudi for the half-year. His note indicates that if the compound interest continues at the current rate for three more years, it will fund a new press. The precision of these accounts demonstrates Luca's facility with numbers, deployed here in service of practical monastery management rather than pure contemplation.

A fragmentary sonnet follows, composed at dusk upon returning from the chapel. Luca writes of setting a keystone in the Borgo arch, marking it with his stonemason's cross, and watching the arch sing its weight. He praises the gold leaf of the angel panel in the chapel, whose gilded halo burns with afternoon light, and observes Saturn completing his orbital arc at the seventh house. The sonnet breaks at the volta with what Luca himself annotates as "a bad line," though he notes that "the keystone of the thought holds." He signs the page with the same stonemason's mark he carved that morning, collapsing the distinction between artisan work and literary composition.

Page four presents a Euclidean demonstration of the golden section—the division of a line segment in extreme and mean ratio, which Luca identifies as governing the pentagon and dodecahedron through the phi-ratio. The demonstration breaks off incomplete; Luca has left a placeholder "Q.E.D." at the foot though the proof remains unfinished. A marginal note indicates it is "to be completed from memory, after chapter" and directs the reader to folio V.27 of a vellum codex on the upper north shelf where the full drawing of the dodecahedron inscribed in its sphere may be found.

A letter addressed to Leonardo da Vinci at the Milan court reveals a friendship grounded in shared intellectual concerns. Luca recalls an evening in Leonardo's studio at the Corte Vecchia, where the oil lamp created such complete chiaroscuro that he could see nothing but its flame reflected in the master's eyes. Leonardo spoke then of how the lamp produces not light but the boundary of light, how a studio is made by disciplined shadow rather than illumination. Luca treasures this as a figure for composition itself. He reminds Leonardo of their subsequent walk through Milan's lanes in a "dialogue-street" conversation that moved from drapery mathematics to the soul. The letter's third matter concerns musical theory: Luca has been working with the monochord and finds that the 2:3 fifth sings pure only under Pythagorean tuning. He asks Leonardo to verify this and sends preliminary figures for "the book" by courier, requesting that Leonardo sketch the fifth regular body in his studio's flame and return it.

The workshop inventory, taken on the feast of St. Francis, catalogs the tools and materials of artistic production with the same precision Luca applies to monastery finances. It records a brass wager-pot formerly belonging to the apprentice Tommaso, lost in a dice game to Piero on a triple-six throw and restored when Piero repented. Three sable brushes of fine point rest in linen on the upper shelf, last used on the lute commission. The workshop lute itself sits on the bench beside a nearly exhausted phial of northern varnish, its new boxwood frets carved by Luca himself. Six egg yolks prepared for tempera wait in a small green earthenware jar. The stone slab and muller bear traces of malachite ground fine and lapis ground coarser. The inventory closes with Luca's gift of a new wager-pot to Tommaso to replace the one lost, with the admonition: "Let the apprentice hold both and wager with neither."

A recorded dream reveals the obsessive mathematical vision that underlies Luca's confession. He dreams of a Jacob's ladder extending from the chapel floor beyond the roof beams, its rungs of brass and ash, with numberless ascending angels upon each rung moving in steps so slow they seem motionless. He attempts to count them as he counts rose-window petals but finds the oneiric procession does not yield to enumeration; he reaches twelve and stops. The dream shifts to a night loggia where the seven planets arrange themselves in planetary-hour order. It is Venus's hour, and the planets move soundlessly while Mars lights the eastern arc. A voice declares the planets themselves are rungs of a second, longer ladder of different metal. Finally, Luca walks inside a dodecahedron he drew that afternoon, finding in each of its twelve faces a chamber containing an unfinished vision of one of the elements—water, air, fire, earth—and in the twelfth face the Platonic aether-fifth, which glows pale and sourceless. He wakes with the dodecahedron still holding him, the aether-fifth fading last, and records it as "a ledger of what cannot be reckoned."

The recipe for tempera and gold-leaf laying represents transmitted workshop knowledge, introduced solemnly: "To be copied carefully; in the name of God; so the masters gave it." The pigment receipt specifies lapis lazuli ground one day for the robe's blues, malachite-green ground a further day for meadow, cinnabar-vermilion ground carefully for the wounds (it stains cloth). The proportions for any given panel are never twice the same. The gold-leaf section describes preparing a ground of bole-red on gesso, burnishing it thrice, then breathing on it and laying the gold leaf with an agate burnisher in one motion. The gilding light—properly understood—is not the gold leaf itself but the manner of setting it; the burnisher catches the light last, and the gilder is thus "not the layer of gold-leaf but the servant of the gilding-light." The recipe breaks off mid-sentence in its fourth section, between instructions about a vinegar-drop for the binder and what should have been final instructions on gold-leaf laying. The ingredient list is known but unfinished; the master's hand does not return to complete it.

A sermon fragment preached on the feast of the Guardian Angels addresses the brethren directly. Luca asks them to consider the rose-window overhead, whose twelve-petal tracery catches clearest light at Sext-hour. He confesses to counting its points six times during that office, arriving each time at the same twelve petals, gladder with each confirmation. He invokes Leonardo's Milan studio, where the oil lamp in the corner teaches that chiaroscuro is made by discipline rather than full brightness—God's grace operates likewise, not as noon's full sun but as patient shade. The sermon's third movement presents a probability argument attributed to "our blessed father Pascal of Sansepolcro" (not the Frenchman): the wager for salvation, however small its probability, multiplied by the infinite gain of the next world, always exceeds the finite stake of this life. Any prudent merchant who balanced books as Luca does would make this wager. The probability of salvation times infinite gain is itself infinite against a finite stake—no true wager at all, but a rational certainty.

The architectural specification for rebuilding the chapel of the Visitation displays Luca's facility with practical geometry. The apse proportions derive from an inscribed square within nested circles centered on the altar slab. The central circle, positioned over the elevation wafer at consecration, measures three breaths in diameter (one braccio, two punti in Sansepolcro measure). This establishes the modular unit; nested circles radiate outward from the elevation wafer, each three breaths of the deacon's walk marking one circle. The Borgo arch keystone is specified in sandstone ashlar from the eastern quarry, bearing the mason's cross-mark on its underside, with springs no less than nine braccia. The façade follows the Urbino school's pilaster-order: Doric below, Ionic above, with three entablature lines at base, mezzanine, and cornice. The proportional elevation scales by five from the entablature line between orders. Luca signs as sacristan.

The travel diary records a journey from Sansepolcro to Bologna and return, undertaken with the muleteer Bartolo and a sound grey pack-mule. The carriage fee totals ten and a half scudi for the journey. Luca carries the breviary corner of Psalm 103 in his sleeve, its pricked margin with the five regular solids the only private mark in the book. He follows the Franciscan rule-road, pausing at every wayside shrine with his tertiary cord touching stone while saying a Pater. At Bologna he lodges at the convent; the breviary comes out again for Compline, and he adds one new faint prick for the truncated cube—not a regular body, but standing in stone in the Bologna cloister. The return journey reverses the stages, each wayside shrine observed as before, the tertiary cord passed through his hand at every pilgrim step.

The wager problem, set out in Luca's analytical manner, arose at a Cesena inn between two apprentices playing for a sixty-florin pot. The game required six winning rounds; when a kitchen fire interrupted them, apprentice A had won five rounds, B only three. A always threw first; the dice was fair; no triple-six had appeared. Luca's solution examines the eight equally possible outcomes of the next three rounds: in seven, A wins at least once and takes the pot; only one outcome (B winning three consecutive, like a triple-six) would give B the pot. Therefore A is owed fifty-two and a half florins, B seven and a half. Both accepted this division. Apprentice A then placed his seven florins at the Monte dei Paschi for compound interest at six percent, calculated to bring it above eight florins in three years. Luca reflects that the wager-for-soul operates by identical reckoning: probability of salvation, however small, times infinite gain, set against the finite stake of this life. The probability is never zero; the wager is always prudent.

A Platonic dialogue between Luca and a visiting scholar continues the conversation they began on a Milan walk down the dialogue-street of the Porta Vercellina at evening. They discussed the soul then; Luca now asks about the Jacob's ladder he has since dreamed, with its brass rungs and ascending angels in oneiric step. The scholar explains it is a figure: the rungs represent degrees of abstraction, the angels the clarities gained at each level, the oneiric step how the mind proceeds—not by full waking but by dream-like movement from clarity to clarity. Plato's ladder terminates in a vision received rather than reasoned. When Luca asks reason's duty during this ascent, the scholar turns the figure back on Luca's own work: Is not the chapel's borgo façade, with its pilaster-order and proportional elevation, reason's work in stone? The façade's pilasters give the ladder-rungs visible body; the entablature line is the oneiric step made permanent; the proportional elevation is itself a Jacob's ladder. Mason and ascending angels do the same work in different matter. Their Milan walk continues on this dialogue-street, only in another city.

A prayer composed after Compline addresses the gold leaf of the angel panel at the high altar, shining in late light. Luca sees not that the gold is gold, but that the illumined margin where gold leaf meets painted robe shows divine brightness as a gilded halo shows a saint's head. He prays to read Euclid VI.30's division in extreme and mean ratio as a letter in God's handwriting. The golden section is not God himself, but the phi-ratio traces an order that is His. When Luca draws it at his bench, it speaks of how the greater relates to the whole as the lesser to the greater—a small catechism in the geometers' tongue. He asks to be kept on the Franciscan rule-road, his pilgrim step true, kneeling at every wayside shrine, his tertiary cord properly knotted at the hip. If he travels rightly, each wayside shrine becomes a small altar, the cord reminds him he is tertiary not master, and the road itself leads eventually to the gold leaf of God's angel panel in last light. He begs forgiveness for pride in geometry and gladness in the gilded halo, and for the pricking at Psalm 103 though absent from this prayer. If at the end the gold leaf is the last thing his eyes see, let its illumined margin be the gate.

An astrological note for the week beginning September eighth records Saturn standing at the seventh house, completing his quartering on Thursday. Saturn's orbital arc is slow; the quartering falls on Mars's hour; the seventh house will hold Saturn most of the week. The seven planets are well ordered, progressing through their planetary hours from Saturn at dawn through Jupiter, Mars, Sol, Venus, Mercury, Luna. Venus's planetary hour falls at Tuesday noon; Luca experienced a quiet Venus-dream with no augury, only the planetary hour manifesting in sleep. Mars-augury is expected later when Mars's planetary hour coincides with the quartering's end; such dreams leave a red edge and tire the sleeper, unlike Venus-dreams that rest. Luca's star-chart matches the Ptolemy Almagest in the library; he has added a margin note directing readers to the zodiac-table at folio two verso. He notes for chapter that Thursday's Saturn planetary hour coincides with chapter itself; Father Bartolomeo should be warned that the planets indicate caution in speech that day, Saturn's weight on words and subsequent Mars-augury likely to disturb the week if provocations are given.

The epitaph Luca composes for his own tomb declares simply: "Here lieth Fra Luca, sacristan of this convent. He kept the balanced-book." The final reckoning of his accounts closed without dispute, debit column carrying three small sins, credit column his longer labors, both columns agreed by Father Bartolomeo, the balanced-book signed and sealed, ruled with a single line at the foot. This is no ordinary balanced-book but one that closes a life, the final reckoning for God. Luca acknowledges he demonstrated much and concluded little. Where his proof margin needed one more Euclidean lemma to complete a broken demonstration, it remained unfinished. The Q.E.D. beneath his last theorem was written in hope, not proof. The proof margin of his last folio holds only a half-lemma; the Euclidean lemma is unsupplied; the Q.E.D. stands alone above the broken demonstration. He asks prayers for the unearned Q.E.D., for the proof margin that holds the lemma's absence. The tomb inscription has been cut by the mason who cut the borgo arch. At noon on the patron's feast, a light beam through the south window strikes the inscription and moves down its length; the lettering has been deepened to catch each letter in turn. The Roman hand lettering spans five lines; each evening's last light leaves this inscription last among the chapel's. A smaller hand notes that the mason Marco cut the lettering to design, Luca checked the inscription, and the light beam was verified at equinox.

A table of musical proportions maps intervals to their ratios: octave 2:1, fifth 3:2, fourth 4:3, tone 9:8, fifth upon fifth 9:4, minor third 6:5. The monochord's gut string, stretched between bridges and tuned to the fundamental, gives the 2:3 fifth when the bridge divides it in that ratio. Pythagorean tuning proceeds from this: each string tuned by ear to the 2:3 fifth of its neighbor, all intervals following from repeated fifths. The monochord is "a small instrument of reason," the gut string its single voice, Pythagorean tuning its first catechism. The workshop lute beside it requires more complex fingering. Its frets are placed so that when the sable brush dusts during cleaning, the fret pattern becomes visible as a ladder. The brush used for the last varnish pass sits with the nearly empty varnish phial on the bench; the lute has had three winter coats, which must cure a fortnight before playing. A four-bar fugue subject has been worked through winter on this lute. Each counterpoint line answering the subject must rise a fifth or fall a fourth; the 9:8 interval serves as passing tone without completing the cadence. Three counterpoint entries are complete; the fourth—here the text breaks off. The fugue subject's fourth counterpoint line is unwritten; the 9:8 interval passes upward but the cadence is broken, cut short, leaving the subject suspended above the final. No full close has been found
